review_type: Scoped critical literature review; not exhaustive systematic review

records.title: Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation
records.venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association 102(477), 359-378
records.support: Proper scoring rules provide an established way to evaluate probability forecasts.
records.counter: Low entropy is not a score for predictive correctness; a concentrated belief can be wrong.
records.implication: Evaluate interpretation probabilities using held-out outcomes and proper scores, alongside calibration plots. Do not validate probabilities by showing that entropy decreases.

records.authors: Bauer, A.; Leucker, M.; Schallhart, C.
records.title: Runtime verification for LTL and TLTL
records.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology 20(4), Article 14
records.support: Runtime verification makes the treatment of finite observations explicit, including inconclusive observations.
records.counter: A finite prefix with an unfinished obligation need not provide the same evidence as a completed satisfying execution.
records.implication: State whether traces are complete finite executions or prefixes. Compare the existing weak-boundary acceptance with a separately specified monitoring interpretation; do not call the existing FRET semantics incorrect.

records.authors: Grenn, M. W.; Sarkani, S.; Mazzuchi, T. A.
records.title: The Requirements Entropy Framework in Systems Engineering
records.support: Entropy has already been applied to requirements populations and their quality-state evolution in systems engineering.
records.counter: The broad claim that requirements entropy is new is untenable. Its random variable differs from a distribution over formal meanings.
records.implication: Position this study as a specific formal-semantics and clarification investigation. Explain why its entropy cannot be compared numerically with a requirements-quality-state entropy.

records.title: A Survey and Classification of Controlled Natural Languages
records.support: Controlled languages offer a mature foundation for balancing natural-language accessibility and formal precision.
records.counter: Restricted syntax and formal precision do not establish that the selected sentence captures a stakeholder intention.
records.implication: Separate grammatical well-formedness, semantic interpretation and validated intent in the user interface and study outcomes.

records.authors: Autili, M.; Grunske, L.; Lumpe, M.; Pelliccione, P.; Tang, A.
records.title: Aligning Qualitative, Real-Time, and Probabilistic Property Specification Patterns Using a Structured English Grammar
records.access: Author project description and institutional metadata
records.support: A structured English grammar can connect qualitative, timed and probabilistic specification patterns.
records.counter: Pattern-based formalization is established; probability inside a system property is different from uncertainty about which property a person intends.
records.implication: Keep operational probabilities and analyst interpretation probabilities separate. Use a varied pattern benchmark rather than only two response examples.

records.title: An NLP approach for cross-domain ambiguity detection in requirements engineering
records.support: Domain-dependent language models support detecting terms whose interpretations may differ across stakeholder domains.
records.counter: Formal candidate enumeration alone does not capture all contextual or terminological ambiguity.
records.implication: Include domain experts and an NLP ambiguity baseline. Record omitted interpretations instead of treating a small generated candidate set as proof of low ambiguity.

records.authors: Cavezza, D. G.; Alrajeh, D.; Gyorgy, A.
records.title: A Weakness Measure for GR(1) Formulae
records.support: Quantitative logical weakness has a formal literature connecting entropy, language properties and specification refinement.
records.counter: Entropy alone can be insufficient for distinctions involving fairness; this work uses additional structure including Hausdorff dimension. Its infinite-language setting differs from this prototype.
records.implication: Do not rename a bounded log model count as a general logical-weakness measure. Test implication, horizon sensitivity and fairness-related limitations separately.

records.authors: Giannakopoulou, D.; Pressburger, T.; Mavridou, A.; Schumann, J.
records.title: Automated formalization of structured natural language requirements
records.support: FRET supplies the structured-language formalization foundation and compositional temporal semantics used by the prototype.
records.counter: Correct translation is a different claim from correct elicitation of intent. The compiler and formalization are prior work.
records.implication: Attribute FRET explicitly, retain compiler provenance and describe entropy analysis as a companion extension rather than a replacement formalization method.

records.title: Natural Language Processing for Requirements Engineering: A Systematic Mapping Study
records.access: Publisher metadata and selected record material
records.support: The mapping study locates requirements-language processing within a substantial prior research landscape.
records.counter: A toy demonstration cannot establish an advantage over the wider NLP-for-requirements literature.
records.implication: Use this survey for backward and forward citation expansion before a submission. This review does not extract numerical effectiveness conclusions from the limited publisher material inspected.

records.title: Aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in machine learning: an introduction to concepts and methods
records.support: The distinction between variability and lack of knowledge helps define what a reported uncertainty number represents.
records.counter: A single entropy value does not automatically isolate epistemic uncertainty or capture model-set incompleteness.
records.implication: Document the uncertain object, probability source and omitted possibilities. Application to requirements elicitation is an inference from this conceptual literature, not an evaluated result of that paper.

records.authors: Montgomery, L.; Fucci, D.; Bouraffa, A.; Scholz, L.; Maalej, W.
records.title: Empirical research on requirements quality: a systematic mapping study
records.support: The mapping study motivates explicit definitions and empirical evaluation of requirements-quality constructs.
records.counter: Ambiguity, consistency, completeness and correctness are distinct. An easily computed scalar is not automatically a validated quality measure.
records.implication: Define an independently judged outcome for each claim. Evaluate whether the entropy measures add information beyond existing defect and quality assessments.

records.authors: Nguyen, V.-L.; Shaker, M. H.; Hullermeier, E.
records.title: How to measure uncertainty in uncertainty sampling for active learning
records.support: Active-learning research studies the consequences of different uncertainty measures for selecting informative observations.
records.counter: Uncertainty sampling and expected information gain are not interchangeable; the best measure depends on assumptions and the task.
records.implication: Compare candidate-selection strategies under answer noise. Do not cite this paper as direct evidence that entropy-ranked FRET questions outperform simpler questions.

records.authors: Farquhar, S.; Kossen, J.; Kuhn, L.; Gal, Y.
records.title: Detecting hallucinations in large language models using semantic entropy
records.support: Grouping outputs by meaning before measuring uncertainty is established in semantic-entropy research.
records.counter: The original setting concerns LLM outputs and particular errors, not stakeholder intention. Semantic entropy itself is not a new contribution here.
records.implication: Study exact bounded formal equivalence, alias-mass conservation and probability calibration as requirements-specific questions. Do not interpret LLM frequency as an automatically valid intent prior.

records.authors: Rainforth, T.; Foster, A.; Ivanova, D. R.; Bickford Smith, F.
records.title: Modern Bayesian Experimental Design
records.support: Expected information gain is a standard objective for selecting experiments that reduce uncertainty.
records.counter: Applying this objective to questions is not, by itself, a new information-theoretic method.
records.implication: Specify priors, answer likelihoods, question costs and decision objectives. A defensible contribution must show a useful requirements-specific method or evaluated benefit beyond this established foundation.

records.authors: Abualhaija, S.; Aydemir, F. B.; Dalpiaz, F.; Dell'Anna, D.; Ferrari, A.; Franch, X.; Fucci, D.
records.title: Replication in Requirements Engineering: The NLP for RE Case
records.venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology 33(6), Article 151, 1-33
records.support: Replication and verifiability require sufficient information about data, annotation and tool reconstruction.
records.counter: A runnable script is useful but does not make an empirical result independently reproducible without the associated protocol and evidence.
records.implication: Release candidate-generation settings, priors, annotation guidance, anonymized answer records where permitted, exclusions and analysis scripts; retain compiler and dataset versions.

records.authors: Henkel, E.; Hauff, N.; Langenfeld, V.; Funk, L.; Podelski, A.
records.title: Is it vacuous to check redundancy, or is it redundant to check vacuity?
records.support: Formal analysis of real-time requirements already addresses redundancy and its relationship with vacuity.
records.counter: A zero marginal trace-count restriction can rediscover bounded redundancy. It does not establish every form of vacuity or unbounded redundancy.
records.implication: Compare quantitative marginal restriction with established logical checks, and label each result by horizon and environment assumptions.

records.authors: Darif, I.; El Boussaidi, G.; Kpodjedo, S.; Politowski, C.
records.title: Controlled Natural Language for Requirements Specification: A Systematic Literature Review
records.venue: ACM Computing Surveys 58(7), Article 175, 36 pages; published January 2026
records.support: A recent review identifies continuing limitations in controlled-language tooling and case-study validation.
records.counter: CNL-based requirements support is an established field; a new interface alone does not resolve its adoption or validation problems.
records.implication: Prioritize evaluation with real users, domain vocabulary and realistic workflows. Avoid interpreting limitations reported in a review as a claim that no successful tools or studies exist.

records.authors: Luckcuck, M.; Sheridan, O.; Farrell, M.; Monahan, R.
records.title: Mu-FRET: a catalogue and tool for requirement refactoring
records.venue: Software and Systems Modeling; online 18 May 2026
records.support: Mu-FRET demonstrates semantics-preserving refactoring and formal equivalence in a FRET-related workflow.
records.counter: Formal comparison of FRET requirements and meaningful tool extensions already exist. Bounded equivalence grouping is not the first semantics-aware FRET extension.
records.implication: Separate changes of wording that preserve meaning from genuinely different candidate meanings; compare grouping against a suitable equivalence baseline.

records.authors: Mendoza, D.; Mavridou, A.; Katis, A.; Trippel, C.
records.title: Automating Requirements Formalization: Using LLMs and Low-Complexity Distinguishing Traces for Semantic Validation
records.support: ARTEMIS combines structured-language candidates, including FRETish, with low-complexity and balanced distinguishing traces.
records.counter: It directly challenges novelty claims for trace-based FRET clarification. Section 7.3 uses an expert specification to answer traces and ensures a plausible candidate is present; effort includes trace-complexity proxies.
records.implication: Use it as a mandatory comparator. Measure actual human accuracy and time, candidate omissions and noisy answers. Do not present the current EIG implementation as the first balanced-trace FRET method.
